q-124105:
An affine transformation $T:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2}$ is a function of the form

$$
x=Au+b,
$$

where $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Notice that we can express the given transformation as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}v-2u-3 \\ u+2v-1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2u+v \\ u+2v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ -1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}\end{aligned}
$$

The transformation $T$ maps the endpoints of $\overset{―}{PQ}$ to the endpoints of $\overset{―}{{P}^{′}{Q}^{′}}.$ So, to find the image of $\overset{―}{PQ},$ we find the images of each endpoint.

To quickly carry out this calculation, we set up the following matrices:

- The matrix $U$ containing the endpoints of our segment:

$$
U=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}]
$$

- The matrix $B$ that has the same shape as $U$ and with the vector $b$ in each column:

$$
B=[\begin{aligned}-3 & -3 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}]
$$

The image of $u$ under $T$ is given by $Au+b.$ So, by applying $T$ to $U,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}AU+B & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-3 & -3 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -5 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-3 & -3 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -8 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the endpoints of the image in the $xy$-plane are $(0,0)$ and $(-8,-1).$

Drawing this segment in the $xy$-plane, we get the following:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14095879/assets/bce5c5155a7e8f1f257b85712627d44dfcc467911a6638016bc3df5892054fef.png)

q-124641:
An affine transformation $T:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2}$ is a function of the form

$$
x=Au+b,
$$

where $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Notice that we can express the given transformation as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2u-v+1 \\ u-v+1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2u-v \\ u-v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}\end{aligned}
$$

The transformation $T$ maps the boundary of $Δ$ to the boundary of the image. So, to find the image of $Δ,$ we find the images of each side.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14095879/assets/c89be48140d49ce8c9def44122aa2bfac779bdd02cfbfbe98f97d414a5637409.png)

          

To quickly carry out this calculation, we set up the following matrices:

- The matrix $U$ containing all vertices of our square:

$$
U=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 2\end{aligned}]
$$

- The matrix $B$ that has the same shape as $U$ and with the vector $b$ in each column:

$$
B=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

The image of $u$ under $T$ is given by $Au+b.$ So, by applying $T$ to $U,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}AU+B & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 2\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & -2\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vertices of the image in the $xy$-plane are $(1,1),(3,2),(1,0),$ and $(-1,-1).$

Drawing this region in the $xy$-plane, we get the following: 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14095879/assets/d038caec0aa360e5d8cc1bcb4a3aa4d88408496d947b312d47634e51bbf4a11f.png)

          

Finally, since $det(A)=-1<0,$ this transformation is not orientation-preserving.

q-124343:
An affine transformation $T:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2}$ is a function of the form

$$
x=Au+b,
$$

where $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Notice that the given transformation is already in matrix form 

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & ={{[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}\end{aligned}
$$

The transformation $T$ maps the boundary of $Δ$ to the boundary of the image. So, to find the image of $Δ,$ we find the images of each side.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14095879/assets/5c38b3ccfc99ca173324e4caf4585e07991162c75741b20b5d288ce73ad0ff98.png)

             

To quickly carry out this calculation, we set up the following matrices:

- The matrix $U$ containing all vertices of our triangle:

$$
U=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 & 2 \\ 1 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}]
$$

- The matrix $B$ that has the same shape as $U$ and with the vector $b$ in each column:

$$
B=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

The image of $u$ under $T$ is given by $Au+b.$ So, by applying $T$ to $U,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}AU+B & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 & 2 & 2 \\ 1 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 & -2 \\ 0 & 2 & 2\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 3 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vertices of the image in the $xy$-plane are $(0,1),(0,3),$ and $(-1,3).$

Drawing this region in the $xy$-plane, we get the following:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14095879/assets/1bcadc0b9909159ebf99280e8d47d52891d2aa8653d9bc89bb2a3bb8363d4fb1.png)

          

Finally, since $det(A)=1>0,$ this transformation preserves orientation.

q-162175:
The matrix representation of the linear transformation associated with $T$ is $A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}].$ 

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we get

$$
det(A)=|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}|=1\cdot 2-(-1)\cdot 1=3.
$$

So, the area scale factor of the transformation is

$$
|det(A)|=|3|=3.
$$

q-162172:
The matrix representation of the linear transformation associated with $T$ is $A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 3 & -1\end{aligned}].$ 

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we get

$$
det(A)=|\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 3 & -1\end{aligned}|=2\cdot (-1)-3\cdot 1=-5.
$$

So, the area scale factor of the transformation is

$$
|det(A)|=|-5|=5.
$$

q-34247:
Using the properties of addition/subtraction and scalar multiplication of vectors to isolate $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}3a+2x & =b \\ 2x & =b-3a \\ x & =\frac{1}{2}(b-3a) \\ x & =\frac{1}{2}([\begin{aligned}24 \\ 8 \\ -15 \\ -2\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -2 \\ -1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]) \\ x & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}12 \\ 14 \\ -12 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\ x & =[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 7 \\ -6 \\ -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=6+7=13.$

q-105157:
Using the properties of addition/subtraction and scalar multiplication of vectors to isolate $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2a+4x & =b \\ 4x & =b-2a \\ x & =\frac{1}{4}(b-2a) \\ x & =\frac{1}{4}([\begin{aligned}14 \\ 2 \\ -2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}5 \\ -3 \\ 1 \\ 6\end{aligned}]) \\ x & =\frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 8 \\ -4 \\ -12\end{aligned}] \\ x & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ -1 \\ -3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

q-115627:
From the diagram we see that the arms of the parabola open to the left. The parabola has its vertex at $(0,0)$ and passes through the point $(-2,3).$

The general standard equation of a parabola whose vertex is $(0,0)$ and whose arms open right or left is given by

$$
{y}^{2}=4px.
$$

Since we know the given parabola passes through the point $(-2,3),$ we can substitute $x=-2$ and $y=3$ into the standard equation and solve for $p:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2} & =4px \\ {3}^{2} & =4p(-2) \\ 9 & =-8p \\ p & =-\frac{9}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the equation of the parabola is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2} & =4px \\ {y}^{2} & =4(-\frac{9}{8})x \\ {y}^{2} & =-\frac{9}{2}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the arms of the parabola open to the left since $p=-\frac{9}{8}$ is negative.

$$
{y}^{2}=4px.
$$

Since we know the given parabola passes through the point $(1,-3),$ we can substitute $x=1$ and $y=-3$ into the standard equation and solve for $p:$

$$

So, the equation of the parabola is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2} & =4px \\ {y}^{2} & =4(\frac{9}{4})x \\ {y}^{2} & =9x.\end{aligned}

Notice that the arms of the parabola open to the right since $p=\frac{9}{4}$ is positive.

q-11809:
From the diagram we see that the arms of the parabola open to the right. The parabola has its vertex at $(-6,0)$ and passes through the point $(-2,6).$

The general standard equation of a parabola whose vertex is $(h,k)$ and whose arms open right or left is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}(y-k)^{2} & =4p(x-h).\end{aligned}
$$

Since we know that the given parabola has its vertex at $(h,k)=(-6,0),$ we substitute $h=-6$ and $k=0$ into the equation above and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2} & =4p(x+6).\end{aligned}
$$

We also know that the given parabola passes through the point $(-2,6),$ so we can substitute $x=-2$ and $y=6$ into the equation above and solve for $p:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2} & =4p(x+6) \\ {6}^{2} & =4p(-2+6) \\ 36 & =16p \\ p & =\frac{9}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the equation of the parabola is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2} & =4p(x+6) \\ {y}^{2} & =4(\frac{9}{4})(x+6) \\ {y}^{2} & =9(x+6).\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the arms of the parabola open to the right since $p=\frac{9}{4}$ is positive.

$$
